title: LCIA Challenge Decision — Decision 5 (18/07/2018)
text:
DECISION RENDERED ON 18 JULY 2018
Subject: The Claimant challenged one of the Arbitrators (nominated by the
Respondent) pursuant to Articles 10.1(iii) and 10.3 of the LCIA Rules 2014.
Outcome: Rejected
Seat: London, England
Governing Law of English law
the Contract:
Summary: The challenge related to the Arbitrator’s appointment as arbitrator
(nominated by the Respondent) in an earlier gas price review arbitration
involving “identical Parties, identical Contract and identical price review
clause”.
The LCIA Court rejected the challenge.
Since London was the seat of the arbitration, the LCIA Court concluded that
English law applied to the extent not modified by the LCIA Rules.
Regardless of how Section 2.1.2 of the Waivable Red List and Section 3.1.5 of
the Orange List of the IBA Conflicts Guidelines are to be construed, the IBA
Conflicts Guidelines do not override English law or the LCIA Rules chosen by
the Parties.
Any prior knowledge of the Arbitrator in the overlapping subject matter in the
two arbitrations was obtained in an adversarial process between the Parties
rather than through “secret ex parte communications.”
The mere fact that the Arbitrator issued the final award in the previous
arbitration was not sufficient to constitute apparent or actual bias barring the
Arbitrator from acting in the second arbitration, even if it involved overlapping
subject matter. A highly respected and experienced arbitrator as the one in
this arbitration should be able to act in accordance with the usual practice of
arbitrators by approaching evidence in the second arbitration with an open
mind, deciding the case afresh based on the material, with which the Claimant
would have a full and fair opportunity to engage.
While the Arbitrator’s letter accepting appointment – and including details on
impartiality and independence – did not acknowledge the overlapping nature
of the subject matter of the two arbitrations, nothing in the letter suggested
that the Arbitrator would examine evidence and submissions on law in the
second arbitration with a closed mind.

While the subject matter of the two arbitrations overlap, “both Parties are in
common and therefore there will be no inside information or inside knowledge
on the part of the Respondent or [the co-arbitrator] which is not known also to
the Claimant.”
The nomination of the same Arbitrator by the Respondent in both arbitrations
was not a breach of the confidentiality provisions in the Parties’ agreement,
which do not purport to restrict any Party’s ability to choose an arbitrator of
its choice.
Decision 5 - 2

The London Court of International Arbitration
LCIA Arbitration No. […]
Between
[…]
Claimant
-and-
[…]
Respondent
Decision on the Challenge
[…]
[…]
18 July 2018
Decision 5 - 3

I Introduction
1. The Claimant is […] a company incorporated in Spain, and is represented by [A]. The Respondent is […]
a company incorporated in Denmark, and is represented by [F].
2. The underlying arbitration relates to a[n] […] agreement for the sale and purchase of [gas] [(the
Agreement)]. (Emphasis added). The [Agreement] contains an arbitration clause providing for
arbitration under the LCIA Rules. The arbitration is seated in London. The [Agreement] is governed by
the laws of England.
3. This arbitration is the second price review arbitration under the [Agreement]. The first arbitration
determined the applicable contract sale price as at, and from, 1 October 2013 (LCIA Arbitration No.[…])
(the First Arbitration), whereas the current arbitration will determine the applicable contract sale price
as at, and from, 1 October 2016 (the Second Arbitration).
4. The Claimant commenced arbitration by a Request, dated 26 December 2017.
5. On 30 January 2018, the LCIA appointed [B] and [C] as two of the three members of the Tribunal upon
the parties’ nomination.
6. On 13 February 2018, the Claimant submitted an application of challenge to [C]’s appointment,
pursuant to Article 10.1 of the LCIA Rules, alleging that the fact [C] was an arbitrator nominated by the
Respondent in the First Arbitration gives rise to justifiable doubt as to [C]’s impartiality and
independence in the arbitral proceeding.
II Background
7. On 9 January 2018, the LCIA informed the parties that the Claimant had nominated [B] and the
Respondent had nominated [C] to serve as arbitrator.
8. On 11 January 2018, the Claimant expressed its concern over the Respondent’s nomination of [C]
because of his serving as an arbitrator in the First Arbitration. The Claimant therefore requested [C] to
decline his appointment.
9. On 12 January 2018, the Respondent submitted comments on the Claimant’s concerns.
10. On the same day, the Claimant objected to the nomination of [C] alleging that the nomination of [C]
would result in a breach of Section 23.6 of the [Agreement]. The Claimant argued that [C] had full
knowledge of the circumstances of the prior arbitration and was therefore “biased with respect to this
arbitration.” The Claimant informed the LCIA that it intended to challenge [C] pursuant to Article 10 of
the LCIA Rules.
11. On 15 January 2018, the Respondent submitted its response to the Claimant’s comment regarding [C]’s
nomination. The Respondent disputed the Claimant’s argument that [C]’s nomination would lead to a
breach of Section 23.6 of the [Agreement]. Further, the Respondent stated that [C]’s participation in
the First Arbitration “would not give rise to any justifiable doubts as to [C]’s ability to decide the Second
Arbitration as an independent and impartial arbitrator, as required by LCIA Article 5.3, based on the
admissible evidence and submissions.”
Decision 5 - 4

12. On 22 January 2018, [C] confirmed his acceptance of office as arbitrator to the LCIA and made the
following disclosure:
Furthermore, as the parties are aware, I have acted as co-arbitrator in LCIA Arbitration No […].
Needless to say, I will in every respect observe my confidentiality obligation following from Art. 30 LCIA
Rules. I will furthermore fulfil the confidentiality requirements pursuant to Sec. 23.6 of [the
Agreement], the purpose of which appears evidently to keep information confidential towards the
market, other competitors and the public and not to exclude arbitrators who were involved in prior
arbitrations.
In particular, as regards my involvement in LCIA Arbitration No […], it is my view that the current and
the completed arbitration concern two different subject matters in that they concern different price
revision time periods.
13. On 13 February 2018, the Claimant submitted an application of challenge to [C]’s appointment,
pursuant to Article 10.1 of the LCIA Rules.
14. On 26 February 2018, in response to the Claimant’s challenge, [C] confirmed that he considered
himself independent and impartial and therefore did not intend to resign from the Arbitral Tribunal.
15. On 27 February 2018, the Respondent submitted its response to the Claimant’s challenge stating that
it did not agree with the challenge.
16. On 14 March 2018, the LCIA appointed [D] to determine the challenge to [C] pursuant to Article 10.4
of the LCIA Rules.
17. On 29 March 2018, per [D]’s direction, the Claimant submitted its reply to the Respondent’s response
to the LCIA.
18. On 12 April 2018, per [D]’s direction, the Respondent submitted its rejoinder to the LCIA.
19. On 19 April 2018, the Respondent submitted the Judgment of the Court of Appeal in H v L [2017] EWHC
137 (Common) (the appeal judgment), to which the Respondent had referred in its response dated 27
February 2018.
20. On that same day, 19 April 2018, the Claimant submitted its response, alleging that the facts in the H
v L case could be distinguished from the present dispute. The Claimant referred to the contents of its
reply in full dated 29 March 2018.
21. On 20 April 2018, the Respondent announced its intention to reply to the Claimant’s response dated
19 April 2018. On the same day, the Claimant stated that the Respondent should not be allowed to
submit a further reply.
22. On the same day, the Respondent submitted its reply referring to several paragraphs of the appeal
judgment in H v L to support its case.
23. On the same day, the Claimant informed the LCIA of its dissatisfaction and disagreement with the
Respondent’s reply. The Claimant further referred to its prior submissions and noted in particular
Decision 5 - 5

paragraphs 81 and 96 of the appeal judgment in H v L.
24. On the same day, the Respondent, in response to the Claimant’s comment, rejected “any charge of
introducing additional allegations or untimely evidence, or unacceptable behaviour.”
III Grounds of the Challenge
25. The Claimant submits that there are circumstances giving rise to justifiable doubts as to [C]’s
impartiality or independence in this arbitration on the following grounds:
(a) [C], having issued the final award as the Respondent’s nominated arbitrator on the Tribunal in the First
Arbitration involving disputes of “identical Parties, identical Contract and identical price review clause”,
will inevitably decide this case influenced by the knowledge he acquired in the First Arbitration;
(b) Respondent’s nomination of [C] is a blatant breach of the [Agreement]’s confidentiality obligations and
[C]’s knowledge of confidential information that he acquired in the First Arbitration generates unfair
and unjustified imbalance in the Tribunal, which may affect the Parties’ right to due process and to
equal treatment; and,
(c) [C]’s response to the Claimant’s objections to his nomination, in his Acceptance letter of 22 January
2018 (the Acceptance Letter) raises justifiable doubts as to his impartiality or independence in this
arbitration.
IV Criteria to be applied
26. Article 10.1(iii) of the LCIA Rules provides that an arbitrator may be challenged if “circumstances exist
that give rise to justifiable doubts as to his impartiality or independence”.
27. In addition, since London is the seat of the arbitration, English law shall apply to this arbitration to the
extent not modified by the LCIA Rules.
28. Section 33(1)(a) of the Arbitration Act provides that “the tribunal shall act fairly and impartially as
between the parties…”.
29. The test under the Arbitration Act is modified by Article 10.1(iii) of the LCIA Rules in that it provides
for a challenge if circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to the arbitrator's
independence, as well as to his impartiality.
30. While Section 33(1)(a) of the Arbitration Act does not require explicitly independence of an arbitrator,
the LCIA Court has ruled, in LCIA Reference No. 8116011, that the Arbitration Act had to be interpreted
in a manner compatible with Article 6(1) of the European Convention on Human rights (the ECHR)
which entitles everyone to a “fair and public hearing ... by an independent and impartial tribunal
established by law.” I note that the English Court in H v L [2018] EWCA Civ 817 [38] took the position
that the English law does not require independence of an arbitrator.
31. The LCIA Court, in its decision in LCIA Reference No. 81160, further held that, applying Article 6(1) of
1 Para. 20, Claimant’s application for challenge
Decision 5 - 6

the ECHR, the English court had revised the test under the Arbitration Act to adopt the test of “whether
the fair-minded and informed observer, having considered the facts, would conclude that there was a
real possibility that the tribunal was biased” (Porter v Magill [2002] 2 AC 357 at [103] per Lord Hope).2
The Parties do not dispute that the test in Porter v. Magill should apply to the present case in
determining the challenge application3. The test is objective and cumulative in that all factors that are
said to give rise to the possibility of apparent bias must be considered cumulatively4.
32. Although I must determine this case in accordance with the LCIA Rules and English law, I have also
considered other materials relied upon by the parties.
33. In particular I have considered the IBA Guidelines on Conflicts of Interest in International Arbitration
2014 (the IBA Guidelines) for guidance as to the parameters of the independence and impartiality of
an arbitrator. The IBA Guidelines provide that:
Doubts are justifiable if a reasonable third person, having knowledge of the relevant facts and
circumstances, would reach the conclusion that there is a likelihood that the arbitrator may be
influenced by factors other than the merits of the case as presented by the parties in reaching his or
her decision5.
34. While I note that the Respondent has not agreed to the application of the IBA Guidelines to this
arbitration and, as it correctly points out, they are mere guidelines and not in any way binding6, the
LCIA Court has referred to the IBA Guidelines in previous decisions on challenges7, as they “reflect
actual practice in a significant part of the arbitration community”8.
35. I also considered the investor-state challenge decisions cited by the Parties.
V Reasoning
36. To begin with, I appreciate the Parties’ detailed submissions, which I found helpful in deciding the
challenge, and I find it appropriate in the circumstances to consider all the submissions made. I do not
refer to every single argument put forward by the Parties in this decision. However, each one of the
points has been taken into account in issuing this decision.
Issues in the challenge applications
37. The issue to be decided is whether the fact that [C] rendered the final award together with the other
Tribunal members in the First Arbitration, either by itself or in conjunction with [C]’s response in his
Acceptance Letter, creates apparent or actual9 bias in relation to the Second Arbitration. As a corollary,
2 R-Ch-Ex-12
3 Para. 5. 3, Respondent's Response; para. 44, Claimant's Reply
4 Para. 45, Claimant's Reply, Para. 16(8), Cofely Limited v. Anthony Bingham [2016] EWHC 240 (Comm) para. 115.
5 Part I (2) (c)
6 Para. 6.1, Respondent’s Response
7 LCIA Challenge Reference 122053 (C-3)
8 Para. 3.7, LCIA Reference No. 81160
9 While the Claimant cited the English court decision (Owners of Catalina and Owners of Norma [1938] 61 Lloyd's
Reps 362-3, para. 20 of Claimant's challenge application) that found actual bias of an arbitrator, it is unclear
Decision 5 - 7

I need to decide whether [C]’s knowledge from the First Arbitration creates an unfair and unjustified
imbalance of information within the Tribunal may affect the Parties’ right to due process and equal
treatment in the Second Arbitration.
Preliminary question
38. As a preliminary issue, the Parties disagree as to whether the First Arbitration and the Second
Arbitration concern substantially the same subject matter. It is true as claimed by the Respondent, that
the First Arbitration and the Second Arbitration deal with different price review periods resulting in
examination of a different set of facts and evidence. The Claimant’s points are equally valid, however,
in that the First Arbitration and the Second Arbitration involve a similar exercise of selection of data
sources and data in the oil & gas sector that are to be relied on, although the specific data to be
examined and applied will differ. Moreover, the selection and application of data sources and data will
be dictated by the same gas price review provision in the same contract. Accordingly, there is
substantial level of overlap of the subject matter in the First Arbitration and the Second Arbitration.
Prior Involvement in the overlapping subject matter as arbitrator
39. Amec Capital Projects Ltd. v Whitefriars City Estates Ltd. [2004] EWCA Civ 1418, and H v L [2017] EWHC
137 (Comm) and its appeal judgment, demonstrate that under English law the standard for a successful
challenge of an arbitrator on the basis of serving as arbitrator in multiple proceedings is high, even
when they involve overlapping subject matters.
40. In Amec, the original decision of an adjudicator was set aside due principally to procedural defects in
his original appointment. He was reappointed when those procedural defects were cured but was
challenged on the basis he would be deciding for a second time the same issues between the same
parties. In applying the objective test of apparent bias, the English court held that “[t]he mere fact that
the tribunal has decided the issue before is therefore not enough for apparent bias. There needs to be
something of substance to lead the fair−minded and informed observer to conclude that there is a real
possibility that the tribunal will not bring an open mind and objective judgment to bear”10.
41. The English courts adopted a similar approach in H v L, in which an insured challenged the presiding
arbitrator who, without disclosing the fact to the insured, accepted appointment as an arbitrator
appointed by the same insurer in another arbitration involving disputes arising out of the same
incident under the same “Bermuda Form” contracts. Popplewell J opined11:
The informed and fair-minded observer would not therefore regard M as unable to act impartially in
the reference between H and L merely by virtue of the fact that he might be an arbitrator in other
references arising out of the incident, and might hear different evidence or argument advanced in
another such reference. The objective and fair-minded assessment would be that his experience and
reputation for integrity would fully enable him to act in accordance with the usual practice of London
arbitrators in fulfilling his duties under s. 33 by approaching the evidence and argument in the H
reference with an open mind; and in deciding the case, in conjunction with the other members of the
whether the Claimant contends actual bias of [C]. However, out of precaution and for the sake of completeness,
I analyzed and determined whether there is any actual bias of [C] in this challenge decision.
10 Para. 21 (R-Ch-Ex-15)
11 This High Court judgement was upheld in H v L [2018] EWCA Civ 817.
Decision 5 - 8

tribunal, in accordance with such material, with which H will have a full and fair opportunity to
engage12.
42. The facts of the present case are distinguishable from the facts of H v L in that, for example, here both
parties were involved in the First Arbitration. Moreover, because the LCIA Rules did not apply to either
the adjudication or arbitration at issue in those cases, on top of the number of unique and different
aspects13 of these cases as compared to the present case, I am not fully convinced that these court
judgements are as decisive as claimed by the Respondent. I also note that the English Court in H v L
took the position that the English law does not require independence of an arbitrator which the LCIA
Rules require.
43. Having said that, in these judgments the English courts have taken a consistent position that the mere
fact of appointment and decision making in overlapping references does not give rise to justifiable
doubts as to the arbitrator’s impartiality. It is striking that the Claimant failed to submit a single English
court judgment or a challenge decision by a Division of the LCIA Court in a challenge decision that
recognized apparent or actual bias of an arbitrator who decided an issue in one party’s favour in a
previous arbitration and subsequently served as an arbitrator appointed by such party in another
arbitration involving overlapping subject matter.
44. The LCIA Court, deciding the challenge under the UNCITRAL Rules14, also dismissed a challenge
application which was made on a basis of an arbitrator’s knowledge in other arbitrations involving
related subject matter. In particular, in the challenge decision rendered by a Division in the LCIA
Reference UN101693 conducted under UNCITRAL rules15 the claimant challenged an arbitrator
nominated by the respondent in three related arbitrations. The claimant contended that an arbitrator’s
ability to evaluate afresh the evidence and submissions on law that he was to hear in the present
arbitration would be hampered by his appointment to the previous two arbitrations between the same
parties with regard to similar issues, most likely involving some or all of the same witnesses appearing
on both sides.
45. The Vice President of the LCIA Court dismissed the challenge16, reasoning that:
I consider that, to the extent there would arise an advantage for [the Respondent’s appointed
arbitrator] vis-à-vis his co-arbitrators (because of knowledge acquired by him in the previous two
arbitrations), I cannot accept that this would, in and of itself, affect [the Respondent’s appointed
arbitrator]’s impartiality and independence. It may happen that one arbitrator has knowledge that
12 Para. 29 (R-Ch-Ex-13)
13 The Amec case involves an adjudicator whose original appointment was not in compliance with the agreement,
which designated a non-existent person as an adjudicator. The adjudicator’s decision was set aside due to the
non-compliance with the parties’ agreement. However the adjudicator was reappointed because, when his
original decision was set aside, the adjudicator candidate who was misnamed in the parties’ agreement passed
away. In H v L the Court of Appeal found a limited degree of overlap between the two references in which the
arbitrator sat with one party in common: H v L [2018] EWCA Civ 817, at [81]. I note also that the decision may
be the subject to a further appeal.
14 The basis for challenge under the UNCITRAL rules were essentially the same as that under the LCIA Rules,
namely whether “circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to the arbitrators impartiality or
independence.”
15 R-Ch-Ex-18
16 Para. 22 (R-Ch-Ex-18)
Decision 5 - 9

another member of the arbitral tribunal does not have. This, absent other circumstances, is not a
reason to remove the arbitrator. Prior knowledge limited to one arbitrator might be a problem if it is,
for example, tainted because it was obtained ex parte or there are other reasons that may give rise to
justifiable doubts about the arbitrator’s impartiality or independence, but not merely because other
members of the tribunal do not have that knowledge. In this case, it followed from the circumstances
of the case that both [the Claimant’s appointed arbitrator] and [the Respondent’s appointed
arbitrator] have, or will have had, prior knowledge about which the Claimant is concerned. However,
it can be assumed that the knowledge has been, or will have been, obtained in an inter partes
adversary process…
46. The present case is similar to the facts in the above decision reached in the UNCITRAL case
administered by the LCIA Court in that any prior knowledge of [C] in the overlapping subject matter in
the two arbitrations was obtained in an inter partes adversarial process rather than through secret ex
parte communications.
47. English courts do recognize that the parties have a legitimate concern in overlapping arbitrations
involving a common arbitrator with only one common party17. In the present case, however, while the
subject matter of the two arbitrations overlap both parties are in common and therefore there will be
no “inside information” or “inside knowledge” on the part of the Respondent or [C] which is not known
also to the Claimant.
48. As such, according to the English court judgments referred to and the previous decision rendered by a
Division of the LCIA Court in the case under the UNCITRAL Rules, under the given circumstances the
mere fact that [C] issued the final award in the First Arbitration is not sufficient to constitute apparent
or actual bias, barring him from serving as an arbitrator in the Second Arbitration even if it involves
overlapping subject matter. A highly respected and experienced arbitrator such as [C] should be able
to act in accordance with the usual practice of arbitrators by approaching evidence in the Second
Arbitration with an open mind, deciding the case afresh based on the material, with which the
Claimant will have a full and fair opportunity to engage.
49. The Claimant emphasizes the special nature of gas price review disputes, highlighting the risk of
generating a “hired arbitrator” by allowing appointment of the same co-arbitrator more than once for
arbitrations under the same price review provisions of the same contract. This argument is not
convincing, as the Claimant assumes reappointment by itself automatically creates apparent or actual
bias of the reappointed arbitrator. Whether reappointment creates apparent or actual bias of the
reappointed arbitrator should be reviewed and decided taking into account specific circumstances.
50. This conclusion is reinforced by the fact that in the [Agreement] the parties specifically agreed that the
chair of the tribunal must not have acted as arbitrator of either Party in an earlier arbitration.
Significantly, in my view, the [Agreement] does not impose the same restriction for a party nominated
arbitrator. The Parties could have, but chose not to agree the same prohibition for party-nominated
arbitrators. Whilst silence of the [Agreement] does not automatically imply that each Party is entitled
to re-nominate the same arbitrator multiple times in the gas price review arbitrations under the
[Agreement], it does suggest that the parties did not intend to preclude the same arbitrator being
nominated by a party more than once.
17 English courts however do not find such sense of unease amounts to justifiable doubts as to the arbitrators’
impartiality.
Decision 5 - 10

51. Also relevant on this point is the fact that the Claimant has repeatedly expressed its profound respect
for [C] as a highly reputable experienced arbitrator with special expertise in the oil & gas sector.
52. In all the circumstances I conclude that the fact of [C] having issued the final award in the First
Arbitration is not sufficient to raise justifiable doubts as to his independence or impartiality. It is
relatively unusual for an allegation of actual bias to be made. Beyond and to the extent such an
allegation is made here it is based on the same facts as those which are said to give rise to apparent
bias. For the reasons given, I do not consider a challenge based on either allegation should succeed.
Further no allegations have been made that [C] lacks independence, which go beyond the claimant's
allegations of impartiality so as to raise concerns under Art. 10. 1 of the LCIA Rules.
Alleged Imbalance of knowledge in the Tribunal
53. Given that I have found no apparent or actual bias of [C], there is no unfair and unjustified imbalance
in the Tribunal. This is supported by a decision rendered by a former Vice President of the LCIA Court
in another challenge decision concerning an UNCITRAL case (LCIA Reference UN101693). After all, [C]
together with the other Tribunal members will decide the Second Arbitration based on the evidence
and arguments to be submitted in the Second Arbitration, just like any other Tribunal member would.
54. While each case needs to be considered on its own merits, an imbalance of knowledge within the
Tribunal is unlikely to arise where, as here, the Claimant was privy to the First Arbitration and is fully
aware of the basis on which [C] came to the conclusion in the First Arbitration.
The Confidentiality Provisions in the [Agreement]
55. The Claimant submits that the confidentiality provisions in the [Agreement] preclude a party’s ability
to nominate the same co-arbitrator in the gas price review arbitration under the [Agreement] and the
Respondent is in breach by nominating [C] in the Second Arbitration.
56. The Claimant appears to contend that the confidentiality provisions in the [Agreement] prevent a Party
from disclosing any Confidential Information submitted to the tribunal in the First Arbitration to the
tribunal in the Second and therefore, those confidentiality provisions practically preclude a Party’s
ability to nominate the same co-arbitrator in the gas price review arbitration under the [Agreement]18.
57. The Claimant’s contention is not convincing. A literal interpretation of the confidentiality provisions in
the [Agreement] is likely to lead to the conclusion that the confidentiality provisions are aimed at
protecting the Confidential Information provided by the other Party, including that submitted in the
arbitration proceedings under the [Agreement] from disclosure to a third party and that they do not
purport to restrict the Parties’ ability to choose an arbitrator of its choice. On this point I concur with
the Respondent and [C]. At the very least, [C] in the Acceptance Letter expressed his commitment to
observe his confidentiality obligations.
[C]’s Responses in his Acceptance Letter
18 Paras. 28-30, Claimant’s Reply
Decision 5 - 11

58. The Claimant submits that [C]’s Acceptance Letter, in which he expressed in a non-neutral manner his
observations on the interpretation of Section 23.6 of the [Agreement] and the subject matter of this
dispute in favour of his appointment, suffices to evidence the objective and legitimate grounds for
concern arising from his appointment in this arbitration19. I disagree.
59. In response to the Claimant’s concerns with respect to the Respondent’s nomination of him, based on
his involvement in the First Arbitration, expressed in the Claimant’s letters dated 11 and 12 January
2018, [C] in the Acceptance Letter gave assurance to the Claimant of his compliance with the
confidentiality obligations under Art. 30 of the LCIA and Section 23.6 of the [Agreement] and shared
his observations on his impartiality and independence in the Second Arbitration. While he did not
acknowledge the overlapping nature of the subject matter of the two arbitrations in the Acceptance
Letter nothing in the Acceptance Letter suggests that [C] would examine evidence and submissions on
law in the Second Arbitration with a closed mind.
IBA Guidelines
60. The Claimant relies on the IBA Guidelines, particularly Section 2.1.2 of the Waivable Red List and
Section 3.1.5 of the Orange List, which provide:
Waivable Red List
2.1.2 The arbitrator had a prior involvement in the dispute.
Orange List
3.1.5 The arbitrator currently serves, or has served within the past three years, as arbitrator in
arbitration on a related issue involving one of the parties, or an affiliate of one of the parties.
61. In respect of Section 2.1.2 of the Waivable Red List, the Parties disagree as to whether this
encompasses a situation where there are successive gas price review disputes under the same contract
or where the arbitrator had a prior involvement in the dispute as an arbitrator, by citing legal
authorities of highly regarded arbitration practitioners20.
62. This is an interesting issue. However, I am not called upon to decide it because even assuming they are
to be treated as the same dispute on the basis of the applicable standards presented before me,
neither English law nor the LCIA Rules find apparent bias of an arbitrator based on the mere fact that
he or she was previously involved in the dispute as arbitrator. Regardless of how Section 2.1.2 of the
Red List is to be construed, the IBA Guidelines do not override English law or the LCIA Rules chosen by
the parties21.
63. In respect of Section 3.1.5 of the Orange List, the Parties are in dispute as to whether Section 3.1.5
encompasses a situation where the arbitrator has served within the past three years, as arbitrator in
19 Paras. 15-21, Claimant’s Reply
20 Page 1868, Gary. B. Born, International Commercial Arbitration (2nd, Kluwer) (R-Ch-Ex-16), Teresa Giovannini,
'Chapter 11: Annulled International Arbitral Awards and Remand: Can/Should the Same Arbitral Tribunal Take
the Case Anew? A Short Analysis from a Swiss Perspective', in Patricia Shaughnessy and Sherlin Tung (eds), The
Powers and Duties of an Arbitrator: Liber Amicorum Pierre A. Karrer, (Kluwer Law International 2017) p. 104 (C-
4).
21 Para.6, Introduction of the IBA Guidelines
Decision 5 - 12

another arbitration on a related issue involving both of the parties, not just one of the parties.
64. Again while this is an interesting issue I am not called upon to decide it in this case either.
65. At the outset, as correctly pointed out by the Respondent, the Orange List compiles “specific situations
that, depending on the facts of a given case, in the eyes of the parties, give rise to doubts as to the
arbitrator’s impartiality or independence”22. An arbitrator has a duty to disclose such circumstances as
fall within the Orange List. However, the test of impartiality and independence is an objective one
under English law as well as under the IBA Guidelines. The fact that the circumstances fall within the
Orange List does not by itself give rise to justifiable doubts as to the arbitrator’s impartiality or
independence.
66. On the basis of the English court judgements and the LCIA Challenge decisions presented to me,
neither English law nor the LCIA Rules finds apparent or actual bias of an arbitrator based on the mere
fact that he or she has previously served as an arbitrator in another arbitration with regard to an
identical or related issue involving both of the parties23 or one of the parties24, regardless of how
Section 3.1.5 of the Orange List is to be construed.
Investor-State Challenge Decisions
67. The Parties also cited investor-state challenge decisions. However, they disagree as to the value of
challenge decisions in investment treaty arbitration to this case.
68. The Claimant extensively relied on investor-state challenge decisions, inter alia the decision on the
challenge in Caratube25 in which the unchallenged arbitrators disqualified an arbitrator appointed by
Kazakhstan based on the fact that he served as an arbitrator appointed by Kazakhstan in another ICSID
arbitration against Kazakhstan involving essentially the same subject matter.
69. In Caratube the unchallenged arbitrators found “evident or obvious appearance of lack of impartiality”
of Mr. Boesch, the challenged arbitrator in reasoning:
That Mr. Boesch would consider it improper to form any opinion based upon external knowledge is not
to be doubted and neither is his intention not to do so: It remains that Mr. Boesch is privy to information
that would possibly permit a judgment based on elements not in the record in the present arbitration
and hence there is an evident or obvious appearance of lack of impartiality as this concept is
understood without any moral appraisal: a reasonable and informed third party observer would hold
that Mr. Boesch, even unwittingly, may make a determination in favor of one or as a matter of fact the
other party that could be based on such external knowledge.26
70. While this ruling lends support to the Claimant's challenge, I find a stark contrast between the

approach taken by the English courts and that of the unchallenged arbitrators in Caratube in deciding
a challenge application.
71. I concur with the Respondent’s submissions that when a significant body of jurisprudence on conflicts
of interest under English law and under the LCIA Rules relevant to the present case is available, such
jurisprudence should be preferred to the jurisprudence of challenge decisions in investor state
arbitration where the procedural governing law may not necessarily be English law.
72. Again, the English court in Amec and H v L which applied the test of impartiality (but not independence)
did not find apparent bais of an arbitrator on the premise that experienced arbitrators sitting in London
arbitration will approach each case with an open mind and deal with it on the basis solely of the
material submitted to that arbitration, even when the arbitrator served as an arbitrator in another
arbitration involving the same or related disputes.
73. The LCIA Court, by applying the test of independence and impartiliaty in its challenge decision
concerning an UNCITRAL case which involved the same parties and overlappting subject matters in
parallel arbitrations with a common arbitrator (LCIA Reference UN101693) dimissed the challenge,
holding that knowledge and impressions of an arbitrator obtained in related arbitrations, do not by
themselves make such arbitrator biased or less independent, particularly when such knowledge has
been, or will have been, obtained in an inter partes adversary process in the related arbitration
proceedings.
74. In contrast, in Caratube the unchallenged arbitrators are more skeptical about experienced arbitrators’
ability to decide on disputes without applying external knowledge once they are exposed to
documents or information in another arbitration involving the same or related disputes.
75. When the English courts and previous decisions issued by Former Vice Presidents of the LCIA Court
already provide sufficient guidance in deciding the present issue, I see no reason why, in this case, I
should depart from that guidance. I accept there may be cases where, in the particular circumstances,
there may be good reason to examine more closely the need for skepticism expressed in Caratube, but
that is not in my view the case here.
76. In any event Caratube and Ruby Roz can be distinguished in that they dealt with essentially the same
subject matters involving one common arbitrator with only one common party while the First
Arbitration and the Second Arbitration deal with the overlapping subject matter involving one common
arbitrator with two common parties.
VI Decision
77. Having carefully considered the submissions of the Parties, I find no circumstances giving rise to
justifiable doubts as to [C]’s impartiality or independence and therefore conclude that the challenge
to [C] should be dismissed.
78. I declare that the costs and expenses generated by the challenge as well as related legal fees should
be determined as part of the final arbitral award.
